## The concept {#sec-beam-concept}

The rig is one clamped cantilever: length $L$, width $b$, thickness $h$,
cross-section area $A=bh$, second moment of area $I=bh^3/12$, Young's modulus
$E$ and density $\rho$ of whatever material it is eventually machined from —
none of which is decided yet; see @sec-beam-design and @tbl-beam-dims. Strain
gauges sit near the clamped root, where bending strain is largest; a target
for a Hall-effect sensor sits at the free tip, for a non-contact displacement
measurement; a mounting point at or near the tip carries an accelerometer.

## Why a cantilever {#sec-beam-why}

One specimen makes strain, tip displacement and natural frequency all
accessible from the same loading, and the same $L, b, h, E, \rho$ enter all
three relations below. [M1](../experiments/M1-strain-load/index.qmd) reads
strain, [M2](../experiments/M2-hall-displacement/index.qmd) reads tip
displacement, [M3](../experiments/M3-vibration/index.qmd) reads the
free-vibration frequency — and because the three formulas share the same
geometry and the same $E$, each experiment's result is a cross-check on the
other two, not an isolated number.

## The relations {#sec-beam-relations}

### Tip deflection under a tip load

For a cantilever fixed at $x=0$ and free at $x=L$, carrying a concentrated
load $F$ at the tip, the Euler–Bernoulli bending moment is $M(x)=F(L-x)$.
Integrating the curvature equation $EI\,y''(x)=-M(x)$ twice with
$y(0)=y'(0)=0$ gives the deflection at any $x$, and at the tip

$$
\delta = \frac{FL^3}{3EI}, \qquad I=\frac{bh^3}{12}
$$ {#eq-beam-deflection}

### Surface strain under a tip load

At the outer fibre, a distance $c=h/2$ from the neutral axis, the bending
strain is $\varepsilon(x)=M(x)\,c/(EI)$. Substituting $M(x)=F(L-x)$ and
$I=bh^3/12$,

$$
\varepsilon(x) = \frac{6F(L-x)}{Ebh^2}
$$ {#eq-beam-strain}

Strain is largest at the root ($x=0$) and falls linearly to zero at the tip
— which is why the gauges sit as close to the root as the clamp allows.

### First natural frequency

For the same uniform cantilever, the first-mode natural frequency is

$$
f_1 = \frac{\lambda_1^2}{2\pi L^2}\sqrt{\frac{EI}{\rho A}},
\qquad \lambda_1 \approx 1.875,\ \ A=bh
$$ {#eq-beam-f1}

with $\lambda_1$ the first root of the cantilever's characteristic equation
$\cos\lambda\cosh\lambda=-1$ [@blevins].

### The stiffness cross-check

@eq-beam-deflection defines a linear tip stiffness $k=F/\delta=3EI/L^3$.
[M1](../experiments/M1-strain-load/index.qmd) fits @eq-beam-strain's slope
$d\varepsilon/dF$ at the gauge position against a set of reference masses;
[M2](../experiments/M2-hall-displacement/index.qmd) fits
@eq-beam-deflection's slope $d\delta/dF = 1/k$ directly. Both slopes contain
the same $E$ and the same $L,b,h$; solving each independently for $E$ and
comparing is the cross-check — and a disagreement between the two, given the
same nominal geometry, is a direct measurement of how wrong "nominal
geometry" actually is (@sec-beam-clamp).

## Design requirements {#sec-beam-design}

Nothing about $L,b,h$ or the material is fixed. What constrains the choice
is a set of inequalities, not a set of numbers.

**Strain must be resolvable but stay elastic.** The strain at the working
tip load $F_\mathrm{work}$, at the gauge position, must sit comfortably
above the smallest strain the [conditioning chain](conditioning-board.qmd)
can resolve, and comfortably below the material's yield strain with a
safety factor $n_\mathrm{sf}$:

$$
\varepsilon_\mathrm{min,resolvable} \;\ll\; \varepsilon(0) =
\frac{6F_\mathrm{work}L}{Ebh^2} \;\le\; \frac{\varepsilon_\mathrm{yield}}{n_\mathrm{sf}}
$$ {#eq-beam-strain-bound}

where $\varepsilon_\mathrm{min,resolvable}$ folds together the bridge
sensitivity (gauge factor, excitation voltage), the [conditioning
board's](conditioning-board.qmd) gain, and the ADC's effective quantization
step — the same kind of quantity
[S1](../experiments/S1-daq-static/index.qmd) measures for the bare
converter.

**The first mode must be sampled adequately but stay clear of the
environment.** Let $f_{s,\max}$ be the highest sustained sampling rate the
chosen board actually achieves — a figure
[S1](../experiments/S1-daq-static/index.qmd) measures, not the one
requested — and $f_\mathrm{env}$ the upper edge of ambient vibration at the
bench (building, footfall, mains-related sources; characterized with the
same accelerometer M3 uses, not assumed). Then

$$
f_\mathrm{env} \;\ll\; f_1 = \frac{\lambda_1^2}{2\pi L^2}\sqrt{\frac{EI}{\rho A}}
\;\ll\; \frac{f_{s,\max}}{2K}
$$ {#eq-beam-freq-bound}

with $K>1$ an oversampling margin beyond the bare Nyquist limit
$f_{s,\max}/2$ — resolving a resonance peak and estimating damping from a
handful of points near it needs more than one sample per cycle at the edge
of aliasing.

@eq-beam-strain-bound and @eq-beam-freq-bound are exactly what tells you
which of $L, b, h$ and which material to pick: they are two inequalities in
five unknowns ($L,b,h,E,\rho$, plus whatever $F_\mathrm{work}$ is chosen),
which is why this page states them and does not solve them — that is the
design step still to do.

::: {.callout-note}
## Tip mass is not in @eq-beam-f1

@eq-beam-f1 is the bare-beam frequency. A Hall-effect target and an
accelerometer mounted at the tip add a concentrated mass there, which is not
part of the uniform-beam derivation and lowers $f_1$ below what
@eq-beam-f1 alone predicts. Treat the formula as a starting point for
sizing, not as the frequency the rig will actually show — that has to be
measured, same as everything else on this page.
:::

## The clamp {#sec-beam-clamp}

The single largest source of disagreement between
@eq-beam-deflection–@eq-beam-f1 and what the rig actually shows is the
boundary condition at $x=0$. The formulas assume a perfectly rigid clamp —
zero rotation, zero translation — and a real clamp is neither: it has finite
stiffness, it has its own mass, and where it stops being "clamp" and starts
being "beam" is not the same as where a ruler says the clamp's edge is.

What this does, in order of importance:

1. **Softens the boundary.** A clamp with finite rotational stiffness
   behaves like a torsional spring in series with the beam, increasing
   measured deflection and strain above @eq-beam-deflection and
   @eq-beam-strain for the same $F$, and lowering $f_1$ below @eq-beam-f1.
2. **Moves the effective root.** If the clamp does not grip cleanly at a
   single cross-section, the beam's effective length $L_\mathrm{eff}$ is not
   the protruding length a ruler measures. Fit $L_\mathrm{eff}$ from the
   data — from @eq-beam-deflection or @eq-beam-f1, with $E$ known some other
   way — rather than assuming it equals the physical protrusion.
3. **Adds its own dynamics.** A clamp with mass and stiffness has its own
   resonance; if that resonance is not well above $f_1$, it couples into the
   measurement instead of behaving as a rigid boundary [@ewins]:
   $$
   f_\mathrm{clamp} \gg f_1
   $$ {#eq-beam-clamp-freq}

Because none of this can be designed away completely, the practical response
is to **measure repeatability**: unclamp and re-clamp the beam several
times, repeating a stiffness or frequency measurement each time, and report
the spread as part of the uncertainty budget rather than assuming a single
clamping event is representative.
